Key Policies.description:
Key policy consists of all the permissions that is applied to a given label.
In simple terms, it is the mapping of label to their permissions.
These Permissions would be for clients, users and groups. It specifies which clients, users, or
groups have permission to use the key, read key, sign key, etc.
So, whenever an operation is performed on a key, all labels applied on this key are fetched.
After that, all key policies related to these labels are computed which decides whether the client, user or a
group is authorized to performed the operation or not.
NAE/KMIP clients work on user based context i.e. they perform operations on behalf of a user. To grant
permissions to NAE/KMIP client, permissions to NAE/KMIP client’s respective user has to be granted, instead of
the client itself.

    {
          "clients": {
            "UseKey": [],
            "ReadKey": ["ClientID"],
            "SignWithKey": [],
            "DecryptWithKey": [],
            "EncryptWithKey": [],
            "SignVerifyWithKey": [],
            "MACWithKey": [],
            "MACVerifyWithKey": [],
            "ExportKey": [],
            "UploadKey": []
          },
          "groups": {
            "UseKey": [],
            "ReadKey": ["Application Data Protection Admins"],
            "SignWithKey": [],
            "DecryptWithKey": [],
            "EncryptWithKey": [],
            "SignVerifyWithKey": [],
            "MACWithKey": [],
            "MACVerifyWithKey": [],
            "ExportKey": [],
            "UploadKey": []
          },
          "users": {
            "UseKey": [],
            "ReadKey": ["UserID"],
            "SignWithKey": [],
            "DecryptWithKey": [],
            "EncryptWithKey": [],
            "SignVerifyWithKey": [],
            "MACWithKey": [],
            "MACVerifyWithKey": [],
            "ExportKey": [],
            "UploadKey": []
          }
    }

Secrets.description:
Secrets are  managed objects that can store user defined data. This data
can be a blob, a password, or a seed (see the `dataType` attribute).
There are two types of objects used to store secrets: a "Secret Object"
and an "Opaque Object"

A "Secret Object" is a password or seed data type.  The seed may be used
for cryptographic operations in the future, which is why it is a separate
type.  The password is a convenient way to store simple text strings.

An "Opaque Object" is a blob data type.  It can be used to store
arbitrary data.

Secrets support many of the same attributes that keys do. They can be
made un-deletable, support meta-data, etc.  They also support most of the
same lifecycle states as keys.

Templates.description:
It is a named Managed Object containing the client-settable attributes of a Managed Cryptographic Object.
A Template is used to specify the attributes of a new Managed Cryptographic Object. A template is applied 
to the created object based on the template reference "id" defined in the object  
This is an example of a template resource     

    {
          "name": "template1",
          "description": "test template",
          "meta": {
            "color":"red"
          },
          "labels": {
            "team": "sales"
          },
          "key_attributes": {
            "activationDate":  "2024-04-15T14:24:37.436073Z",
            "algorithm": "EC",
            "curveid": "prime256v1",
            "deactivationDate":  "2024-04-16T14:24:37.436073Z",
            "meta": {
              "ownerId": "local|e5bd964d-47d2-4254-a561-55842863868a"
            },
            "processStartDate": "2024-04-15T14:24:37.436073Z",
            "protectStopDate": "2024-04-16T13:24:37.436073Z",
            "size": 256,
            "undeletable": true,
            "description": "KeyUndeletable"
          }
    }      

Only key_attributes defined in the template request will be applied to the object using that template.

Template Update API      
   This is an example of a template update API      

    {
          "description": "test template",
          "meta": {
            "color":"white"
          },
          "labels": {
            "newteam": "sales"
          },
          "key_attributes": {
            "activationDate":  "2024-04-15T14:24:37.436073Z",
            "algorithm": "EC",
            "curveid": "prime256v1",
            "deactivationDate":  "2024-04-16T14:24:37.436073Z",
            "meta": {
              "ownerId": "local|e5bd964d-47d2-4254-a561-55842863868a"
            },
            "processStartDate": "2024-04-15T14:24:37.436073Z",
            "protectStopDate": "2024-04-16T13:24:37.436073Z",
            "size": 128,
            "undeletable": true,
            "description": "KeyUndeletable"
          }
    }


For labels in Update API - these are key value pairs so any Key which is not same
as per existing key , will be merge. If same then value to corresponding key will be updated.


For Example

Scenario 1:      
    existing resource request:
        `{ "team": "sales" }`  
    update API request:
        `{ "newteam": "sales" }`      
    In Update API, there is a new key-value pair. Therefore the response will be:
        `{ "team": "sales"; "newteam": "sales" }`


Scenario 2:      
 If the key remains the same in the Update API, the value of the corresponding key will be updated.      
    existing resource request:
        `{ "team": "sales" }`        
    update API request:
        `{ "team": "hr" }`      
    In Update API, there is a new value for "team". Therefore the response will be:
        `{ "team": "hr" }`

All valid fields such as Meta and key_attributes in the Update API will be updated with the newly defined field values

Template List API Filters          

For labels - The filter matches the selector expression      
  `example: team=sales or team=sales,team!=HR`


For meta and key_attributes - The filter matches the valid jsom      
  `example: meta {"color":"red"}`      
  `example:key_attributes {"algorithm":"AES"}`

Services.description:
Services API can be used to reset a CipherTrust Manager instance, that is, wipe all data in
the CipherTrust Manager, restart CipherTrust Manager services and get their status.

The CipherTrust Manager services that can be restarted with this API are 'NAE' and 'KMIP'.

Interfaces.description:
Interfaces are the services the CipherTrust Manager is hosting.  Most interfaces
are listening on a particular port, but may also represent other input
channels, like local shell access or serial port access.

Currently, there are five default interfaces:

- *web*: The HTTP server on port 80 and 443.  This interface serves
both the GUI and the REST API.
- *nae*: The NAE-XML server, on port 9000.
- *kmip*: The KMIP server, on port 5696.
- *ssh*: The SSH system service, on port 22.
- *preboot*: The HTTP server on port 443 during preboot phase of CipherTrust Manager. During this phase,
CipherTrust Manager is run with reduced set of services to facilitate disk encryption 
management. This preboot interface serves REST API during preboot phase of CipherTrust Manager.

Some interfaces can be added and removed, they are:
- *snmp*: Only running and available when listed as an interface
- *nae*: Additional ports can be allocated for NAE by adding additional
         interfaces

Currently, SSH service on host machines can be enabled or disabled via Enable/Disable Interface feature.
Once disabled, it will block ssh access on the host machine.
This setting will persist on subsequent system restarts.

Default connection:
The default connection may be "local_account" for local authentication or the LDAP domain
for LDAP authentication. This value is applied when the username does not embed the connection
name (e.g. "jdoe" effectively becomes "local_account|jdoe"). This value only applies to NAE
only and is ignored if set for web and KMIP interfaces.

The *mode* Interface configuration parameter specifies the Interface mode, and
must be one of the following:
- *no-tls-pw-opt*: No TLS, allow anonymous logins.
- *no-tls-pw-req*: No TLS, user must supply password.
- *unauth-tls-pw-opt*: TLS, allow anonymous logins, ignore client cert.
- *unauth-tls-pw-req*: TLS, user must supply password, ignore client cert, deprecated and replaced with tls-cert-opt-pw-opt.
- *tls-cert-opt-pw-opt*: TLS, user must supply client cert or password.
- *tls-pw-opt*: TLS, allow anonymous logins, verify client cert.
- *tls-pw-req*: TLS, user must supply password, verify client cert.
- *tls-cert-pw-opt*: Verify client cert, user name taken from client cert, auth request is optional.
- *tls-cert-and-pw*: Verify client cert, password is needed, user name in cert must match user name in authentication request.

Each interface has the following restrictions on the mode:
- *nae*: All modes are allowed except *tls-cert-opt-pw-opt*. Default is *unauth-tls-pw-req*.
- *web*: The only allowed mode is *tls-cert-opt-pw-opt*.
- *kmip*: The only allowed modes are *tls-pw-opt*, *tls-pw-req*, *tls-cert-pw-opt* and *tls-cert-and-pw*. Default is *tls-cert-pw-opt*.
- *snmp*: N/A.
- *ssh*: N/A.
- *preboot*: N/A.

The *tls-pw-opt*, *tls-pw-req*, *tls-cert-req* and *tls-cert-and-pw-req* modes verify that the TLS client
certificate is signed by one of the trusted CAs.

The *tls-cert-req* and *tls-cert-and-pw-req* extract the user name from the certificate.
The *certUserField* Interface configuration parameter specifies how the user name is extracted
from the client certificate. The default value is *CN*. It must be one of the following:
- *CN*: common name
- *OU*: organizational unit
- *SN*: surname
- *E*: email address
- *UID*: user ID
- *E_ND*: email without domain; the data to the left of the @ sign in the email address is taken as the user name.

Hard delete option for KMIP keys:
kmip_enable_hard_delete option enables hard delete of keys on KMIP Destroy operation, that is, both meta-data and
material are removed from CipherTrust Manager for the key being deleted. By default, only key material is removed and meta-data
is preserved with the updated key state. This setting applies only to KMIP interface. Should be set to 1 for enabling
the feature or 0 for returning to default behavior.

TLS Ciphers contain the list of cipher suites available in the system for the respective interfaces (KMIP, NAE & WEB)
for TLS handshake. Every new interface will be created with the default set of cipher suites and can be updated using
update interface API (/v1/configs/interfaces/{interface}).
Removal or addition of any cipher suite is not allowed; cipher suites can only be marked as enabled or disabled provided
they are configurable, and also, order can be changed to set preference order.
TLS 1.3 ciphers suites are not configurable, however, you can disable the TLS protocol as a whole.
Disabling all cipher suites for protocols up to TLSv1.2 is restricted unless respective protocols are disabled.

The CipherTrust Manager system might need to be restarted after any interface update for the new settings to take effect.

Policies.description:
Policies define access control rules.

CipherTrust Manager uses an [Attribute-Based Access Control (ABAC)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Attribute-Based_Access_Control)
system to authorize requests.  ABAC essentially means authorization
decisions are based on the attributes and the entities involved with
the request.  ABAC is a superset of many other authorization frameworks.
For example, RBAC, which makes decisions based on the roles of the
user, is also an ABAC system.  RBAC uses one specific attribute of the
user (roles) to make authorization decisions.

ABAC systems, like CipherTrust Manager, can use any attribute of the request,
the requesting user, or the resources involved, to make the
authorization decision.

CipherTrust Manager's ABAC policy language is based on XAMCL.  The core concept
of the language is the Policy resource.  Policy resources describe the
who, what, where, and when of what is allowed and what is denied.
CipherTrust Manager breaks each request down into a set of discrete *operations*
required to fulfill the request.  For each operation, CipherTrust Manager searches
its database for Policies which match attributes of the operation, and
combines them into an authorization decision.  The decisions for
each operation are combined to issue a final authorization decision for
the overall request.

When a request is received by the system, it translates the request into a
set of *operations*.  An *operation* is a JSON object describing the
request.  Here's an abridged example of an operation:

    {
      "action": "ReadKey",                      // the requested action
      "resource": "a:b:vault:keys:signingkey",  // the target resource
      "context": {
        "principal": {
          // attributes of the requesting user
        },
        "resource": {
          // attributes of the target resource
        },
        "environment": {
          // other request attributes, like time of
          // day, network origin, or request params
        }
      }
    }

There are usually lots of attributes in the `principal`, `resource`, and
`environment` sections.  Here's an example of an actual, complete operation:

    {
      "action": "CreateKey",
      "resource": "kylo:kylo:vault:keys:first-v0",
      "context": {
        "principal": {
          "aud": "4414d7ec-9b80-4bb4-b7a6-4c8ad5648333",
          "sub": "local|dc0d9fa0-a0d3-4b46-baee-cd9e07a3be77",
          "iss": "kylo",
          "acc": "kylo",
          "cust": {
            "groups": [
              "admin"
            ]
          },
          "acct": "kylo:kylo:admin:accounts:kylo",
          "user": "ncryptify:gemalto:admin:users:local-dc0d9fa0-a0d3-4b46-baee-cd9e07a3be77",
          "ident": "ncryptify:gemalto:admin:identities:local-dc0d9fa0-a0d3-4b46-baee-cd9e07a3be77-local-dc0d9fa0-a0d3-4b46-baee-cd9e07a3be77",
          "app": "ncryptify:gemalto:admin:apps:kylo",
          "dev_acct": "ncryptify:gemalto:admin:accounts:gemalto",
          "jti": "7478ba67-26b0-494e-9a9d-bf42c21a8629",
          "jwtid": "7478ba67-26b0-494e-9a9d-bf42c21a8629",
          "signer": "eyJhbGciOiJSUzI1NiIsInR5cCI6IkpXVCJ9..u1HydcVRRciFvtzciv7f-46P4m8jCNFiJFQAMjkdc1niD9yT6cHBqVei86ETGyDOGXX3ztczqiImKd6say95WZxe7CrZTqC6HF_6ZF1rtlSSpPk34yr7HAOz78_4CLksAxfQnt9OX1rriZ_VTloDlMXufEIJzdP-ysKDVVnUeMo",
          "iat": 1485384273,
          "exp": 1485384873
        },
        "resource": {
          "account": "kylo:kylo:admin:accounts:kylo",
          "algorithm": "AES",
          "application": "ncryptify:gemalto:admin:apps:kylo",
          "createdAt": "0001-01-01T00:00:00Z",
          "devAccount": "ncryptify:gemalto:admin:accounts:gemalto",
          "format": "raw",
          "id": "",
          "meta": null,
          "name": "first",
          "size": 256,
          "undeletable": false,
          "unexportable": false,
          "updatedAt": "0001-01-01T00:00:00Z",
          "uri": "kylo:kylo:vault:keys:first-v0",
          "usage": "blob",
          "version": 0
        },
        "environment": {
          "time": "2017-01-25T22:44:33.914124104Z"
        }
      }
    }

A Policy consists of properties describing the attributes of matching
operations, and a rule, which is the effect the Policy has on the
final authorization decision: either allow or deny.  This is an
abbreviated example of a Policy resource which matches the operation
above:

    {
      "allow": true,
      "actions": ["ReadKey"],
      "resources": ["a:b:vault:keys:signingkey"],
      "conditions": []
    }

The system then selects the set of Policies where:

1. the operation's `action` matches one of the Policy's `actions.`
2. AND the operation's `resource` matches one of the Policy's `resources.`
3. AND the operation meets all the Policy's `conditions` (if any).

An operation may match many Policies.  The `allow` properties of the
matching Policies combine to form a final decision.  CipherTrust Manager's
strategy for combining policies is that an operation must match at
least one "allow" policy, and cannot match any "deny" policies.

> Policies by themselves are not immediately enforced, meaning the
> authorization system will ignore them.  Policies need to be assigned
> to a set of users in order to be enforced.  See [Policy Attachments](#Policy_Attachments).

The following sections describe the Policy's properties in more detail.

**`actions`**

The `action` attribute of an operation is a string, in the form of
"VerbResource" (e.g. "CreateKey"), or
"VerbWithResource" (e.g. "EncryptWithKey").  Most of the resource types,
like "Key", "Policy", and "Record" share a common set of verbs: "Read",
"Create", "Update", and "Delete".  For example, the basic set of
actions which target Key resources are:

- CreateKey
- ReadKey
- UpdateKey
- DeleteKey

Some resources support additional verbs.  For example, the following
additional actions apply to Keys:

- ExportKey
- UseKey
- EncryptWithKey
- DecryptWithKey
- SignWithKey
- SignVerifyWithKey
- MACWithKey
- MACVerifyWithKey

The `actions` attribute of Policies is an array of these values,
and may contain wildcards (? or _).  Examples:

    "actions": ["CreateKey"]              // matches "CreateKey"
    "actions": ["CreateKey","DeleteKey"]  // matches "CreateKey" OR "DeleteKey"
    "actions": ["*Key"]                   // matches all actions ending with "Key"
    "actions": ["*"]                      // matches all actions

**`resources`**

The `resource` attribute of an operation is in the form of a
resource URI.  Therefore, the `resources` attribute of Policies is an
array of URIs, and can contain wildcards (? or *).  Examples:

    "resources": ["a:b:c:d:e"]             // single resource
    "resources": ["a:b:c:d:e","x:y:z:w:v"] // multiple resources, matches either
    "resources": ["a:b:*:d:e"]             // wildcard
    "resources": ["*"]                     // matches all resources

**`conditions`**

Conditions are rules for matching the other attributes of the operation.
Remember, an operation is a JSON object describing everything about the
request: the who, what, to what, when, etc.
Conditions use an expression syntax that let you compose complex
matching rules against almost any attribute of the operation.

In the Policy structure, the `conditions` attribute is an array of condition objects.
When evaluating whether a policy matches an operation, any conditions contained in the policy are
also evaluated against the operation.  All conditions must be satisfied for the policy to match,
i.e. the conditions are combined with a boolean AND.

To understand the syntax of a condition, let's look at an
example operation, and a policy which matches the operation.

This is the operation:

    {
      "action": "CreateKey",
      "resource": "kylo:kylo:vault:keys:moms3-v0",
      "context": {
        "principal": {},                  // omitted...
        "resource": {                     // some properties omitted...
          "alg": "aes"
        },
        "environment": {},                // omitted...
      }
    }

This is a matching Policy, with a condition:

    {
      "allow": true,
      "actions": ["*Key"],
      "resources": ["*"],
      "conditions": [
        {
          "path": "context.resource.alg",
          "op": "equals",
          "values": ["aes"]
        }
      ]
    }

This Policy will grant the users to which it is assigned permission
to perform actions matching "*Key", on any resource, with
one condition: the key must have a property named "alg" with the value
"aes".

The condition's `path` is "context.resource.alg".  That is
interpreted as a JSON path, evaluated against the operation object:
`context` -> `resource` -> `alg`, which resolves to a
value of "aes".

The `op` property of the condition is the comparison operator used to
compare the value in the operation with the conditions' values.

The `values` property of the condition can be a single value or an array of
values. If `values` is an array, the values combine with a boolean
OR.  In other words, the operation value is compared
with *each* of the items in the `values` array, and if *any* match, the
condition is met.  If `values` is not an array, it's treated like
an array of one item.

> To disambiguate an array of values from a single value *which
> is an array*, you'll need to nest such values
> inside another array.  As an example, say I want
> to match against users who are members of two, and only two, groups: "hr"
> and "eng".  That condition would look like:
>
>     {
>       "path":"context.principal.groups",
>       "op":"equals",
>       "values":[["hr","eng"]]
>     }
>
> `values` is set to an array with a single item, which itself is an array
> with the two groups in it.  This translates to "`groups`
> must equal an array containing `hr` and `eng`".
> If the condition had been:
>
>     {
>       "path":"context.principal.groups",
>       "op":"equals",
>       "values": ["hr","eng"]
>     }
>
> ...that would translate to "`groups` must equal either `hr`
> or `eng`".

The `op` property is the operator used to compare the operation value
to the condition values.  These are the supported operators:

op | description
--- | ---
equals, == | values must match exactly. Values can be any JSON type (string, int, array, object, etc).
equalsIgnoreCase | like `equals`, but only works with string values
empty | the value must not be present in the operation, or must be equal to `null`, an empty string, an empty array, or an empty object. `values` is ignored.
matches, regex, =~ | `values` should be regex expressions, which are matched against the operation value.  Only works with strings.
contains, @> | The operation value must "contain" the condition value. JSON containment is implemented like postgres' [JSONB containment](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/9.4/static/datatype-json.html#JSON-CONTAINMENT) operator. Briefly, for scalar values, like strings or ints, containment is the same as equality.  For arrays, array A contains value B if either B is a scalar value and present in A, or B is also an array, and all of B's items are also in A. For objects, object A contains object B if all of B's properties are in A, and the A's values for those properties contain B's values for those properties (recursively).

Examples:

    "foo" contains "foo"                                // scalars just use equality
    ["foo","bar"] contains "foo"                        // array contains scalar
    ["foo","bar"] contains ["foo"]                      // array contains array with matching items
    {"color":"red"} contains {"color":"red"}            // objects: properties match
    {"groups":["hr","eng"]} contains {"groups":["hr"]}  // contains is recursive
    [["hr","eng"]] does not contain ["hr"]              // left array does not contain
                                                        // a single scalar value equal to
                                                        // "hr".  but...
    [["hr","eng"]] contains [["hr"]]                    // and...
    ["hr",["it","eng"]] contains ["hr"]

**Template Variables**

Conditions also support the use of "template variables", which are resolved at
the time of the authorization request.  Variables are useful for conditions
that compare one attribute of the request to another attribute of
the request, e.g. to compare an attribute in the target resource to
an attribute of the user making the request.

The `path` and `values` properties of conditions also support the use
of template variables, which are resolved at the time of the
authorization request.  To understand the syntax of template variables,
let's use an example.  A user has made a request, which resulted in
an authorization check on this operation:

    {
      "action": "CreateKey",
      "resource": "kylo:kylo:vault:keys:moms3-v0",
      "context": {
        "principal": {                       // Some properties omitted...
          "groups": ["hr","it"]
        },
        "resource": {                        // Some properties omitted...
          "permissions": {
            "CreateKey": ["it"]
          }
        },
        "environment": {}                   // omitted
      }
    }


Here's an example of a matching policy condition which
uses template variables:

    {
      "path":"context.resource.permissions.{{action}}",
      "op":"contains",
      "values": "{{context.principal.groups}}"
    }

The `path` for this condition contains the template variable `{{action}}`.
When the condition is evaluated, `{{action}}` will be replaced by the
action in the operation, which in this example is "CreateKey".  So
the resolved path will be "context.resource.permissions.CreateKey".

Similiarly, the `{{context.principal.groups}}` variable will be
evaluated against the operation, and will resolve to
`["hr","it"]` (the `groups` attribute of the principal).

Put these together, and the condition could be described as
"The resource's permissions must grant the requested action to one of
the user's groups".

The fully resolved condition would look like this:

    {
      "path":"context.resource.permissions.CreateKey",
      "op":"contains",
      "values": ["hr","it"]
    }

Because `values` are combined with a boolean OR, this condition means
that the array of group names at `context.resource.permissions.CreateKey`
must contain one of the group names in the `values` array (any one).

Template variables must be embedded inside string values, and are
enclosed in double curly braces.  The value inside the braces is
a JSON path evaluated against the operation at the time of the request.

> Even though the template variable in `values` was embedded
> in a string, since it resolved to an array, the system replaced the
> string with an array.  If the template variable is the entire value of
> the string its embedded in, the string is replaced with
> the resolved value.  If the template variable is embedded in a string with
> other characters, the overall value will still be a string.

The final, resolved condition is then evaluated against the operation.
Template variables are useful in situations where the condition involves
comparing multiple attributes of the operation to each other.

**Operation Attributes**

The `resource` of the operation will be the same
JSON object that is returned if you GET that resource with the REST
API.  To see the attributes of a resource which can be referenced
in policy conditions, GET that resource.  Here is a complete example
of a Key resource:

    {
      "id": "2ad35187-e180-4339-a36c-a8de9ae6f64b",
      "uri": "kylo:kylo:vault:keys:moms3-v0",
      "account": "kylo:kylo:admin:accounts:kylo",
      "application": "ncryptify:gemalto:admin:apps:kylo",
      "devAccount": "ncryptify:gemalto:admin:accounts:gemalto",
      "createdAt": "2016-12-21T17:24:53.092358873Z",
      "name": "moms3",
      "updatedAt": "2016-12-21T17:24:53.092358873Z",
      "usage": "blob",
      "meta": {
        "ownerId": "local|95a4d02e-2371-422c-bb17-a218ba0375a5"
      },
      "version": 0,
      "algorithm": "AES",
      "size": 256,
      "format": "raw",
      "unexportable": false,
      "undeletable": false
    }

The `principal` of the operation is an object containing
the attributes of the authenticated user.  Use the `/admin/principal`
endpoint to get the principal resource for the current user.
Here's an example of a `principal` resource:

    {
      "aud": "4414d7ec-9b80-4bb4-b7a6-4c8ad5648333",
      "sub": "local|95a4d02e-2371-422c-bb17-a218ba0375a5",
      "iss": "kylo",
      "acc": "kylo",
      "acct": "kylo:kylo:admin:accounts:kylo",
      "user": "ncryptify:gemalto:admin:users:local-95a4d02e-2371-422c-bb17-a218ba0375a5",
      "ident": "ncryptify:gemalto:admin:identities:local-95a4d02e-2371-422c-bb17-a218ba0375a5-local-95a4d02e-2371-422c-bb17-a218ba0375a5",
      "app": "ncryptify:gemalto:admin:apps:kylo",
      "dev_acct": "ncryptify:gemalto:admin:accounts:gemalto",
      "cust": {
        "groups": [
          "admin"
        ]
      }
    }

The `sub` attribute is the user's `user_id`.  `cust.groups` is an array
of the groups of which the user is a member. `aud`,`iss`,`acc`,`acct`,`user`,
`ident`, `app`, and `dev_acct` are reserved for future
use.

Policy Attachments.description:
Policies on their own are not enforced.  Policies have to be assigned to a
set of users first.  This is done by creating Policy Attachment resources.
Here's an abbreviated example of a Policy Attachment:

    {
      "policy": "a:b:admin:policies:admins",
      "principalSelector": {
        "cust": {
          "groups": ["admin"]
        }
      },

      // The following properties are copied from the attached
      // policy.  They are read-only, and included here reduce
      // the number of roundtrips to the API
      "actions": ...,
      "resources": ...,
      "allow": ...,
      "conditions": ...
    }

A Policy Attachment assigns, or "attaches", a single policy, identified
by the `policy` attribute, to a set of
users whose attributes match a selector, known as the `principalSelector`.
This is very similar to the way Policies match the attributes of the
operation.  In fact, a Policy Attachment is virtually identical a policy
condition in the form:

    {
      "path": "context.principal",
      "op": "contains",
      "values": [ {} ]  // the object nested is the principalSelector
    }

The effect of Policy Attachments and conditions overlap: it is possible
to achieve identical effects by attaching a broad Policy to a narrowly
defined Policy Attachment, or attach a Policy with a narrowly defined
condition on the "context.principal" to a broadly defined Policy
Attachment which matches all users.  The redundancy is intentional:

1. Policies are somewhat expensive to evaluate, so the fewer Policies that
need to be evaluated against a request, the better.  Policy Attachments
evaluate faster than Policy conditions, so they can quickly narrow the
set of Policies to evaluate.
2. On the other hand, Policy Attachments do not support template
variables, which are supported in Policy conditions.  Template variables
sometimes reduce the number of Policies required to express complex
authorization rules.  Again, this reduces the number of policies to
evaluate, which increases performance.  Template variables can also
express rules that cannot be expressed with Policy Attachments.
3. Finally, Attachments promote Policy re-use.

To create a Policy Attachment, the request must include the `policy`
and `principalSelector` properties.  The `policy` property can be any
of the policy's identifiers: the `id`, `uri`, or `name`.  After creation,
the `policy` attribute will be the policies `uri`.

The `principalSelector` should include a set of attributes to match
against the principal of an operation.  The system evaluates whether
the principal "contains" the `principalSelector`.  The semantics of the
"contains" operator, and the attributes of principals, are described in
[Policies](#Policies).  To match *all* users, use an empty
`principalSelector`.

The attributes of Policy Attributes which are copied from the
referenced policy do not need to be specified when creating Policy
Attachments.  They are read-only.

For convenience, repeating the same create Policy Attachment request is
allowed, and indempotent.  In other words, if I issue the same create
request three times, containing the body:

    {
      "policy":"admins",
      "principal": {
        "cust": {
          "groups": ["admin"]
        }
      }
    }

...the first request will succeed, creating the Attachment.  The
subsequent requests will also succeed.  They will be no-ops on the server,
and will simply return the existing attachment.

Licensing.description:
Licenses can be installed to enable extended functionality for enterprise level
features such as clustering and external identity provider options, and for various
connectors such as KMIP clients.

By default the system ships with a trial for the enterprise level features, which can be
activated using the `licensing/trials` API.

Licenses are locked to a particular Virtual CipherTrust Manager instance. Get the license lock code using the
`licensing/lockdata` API and use the license lock code on Thales’
Virtual CipherTrust License portal to get the license code. Install the
license using the `licensing/licenses/` API. Installed licenses and
licensed features can be retrieved as well.

The API provides an endpoint for license management.

Syslog Connections.description:
Audit records can optionally be sent to one or more external syslog
server(s). By default audit records are stored in the local database and
will continue to do so even if syslog connections are configured. Each
audit record will be sent to each configured syslog connection.

A syslog connection can either use UDP, TCP or TCP + TLS as the transport
protocol. When TCP + TLS is used a trusted CA certificate in PEM format
must also be provided.

All syslog messages are generated with facility `local0`.

Available log message format are:
* `rfc5424` (default)
* `plain_message`
* `cef`
* `leef`

An example entry looks as follows:

**Plain Message:**
```
2019-08-12 06:25:12 ciphertrust CipherTrust: 2019-08-12 06:25:12 | 'Update Syslog Connection' succeeded ({"createdAt":"2019-08-12T06:25:12.380743Z","details":{"id":"e847e529-d331-45f9-a494-83ee7ce6ab69"},"message":"Update Syslog Connection","service":"kylo","success":true,"username":"admin","severity":"info","clientIP":"","source":""})
```

**RFC5424:**
```
2019-08-12 06:22:16 ciphertrust CipherTrust: <134>1 2019-08-12 06:22:16 ciphertrust CipherTrust - b7999852-dd64-46e9-b924-c3999eca9fad [msg="Update Syslog Connection" sev="6" details="'Update Syslog Connection' succeeded ({"createdAt":"2019-08-12T06:22:16.113081Z","details":{"id":"e847e529-d331-45f9-a494-83ee7ce6ab69"},"message":"Update Syslog Connection","service":"kylo","success":true,"username":"admin","severity":"info","clientIP":"","source":""})"]
```

**CEF:**
```
2019-08-05 11:40:19 ciphertrust CipherTrust: 2019-08-05 11:40:19 ciphertrust CEF:0|Thales Group|CipherTrust|Development|34a71dbf-26d2-47ea-b66d-44e38d0f6c99|Update Syslog Connection|6|'Update Syslog Connection' succeeded ({"createdAt":"2019-08-12T06:14:54.762963Z","details":{"id":"e847e529-d331-45f9-a494-83ee7ce6ab69"},"message":"Update Syslog Connection","service":"kylo","success":true,"username":"admin","severity":"info","clientIP":"","source":""})
```

**LEEF:**
```
2019-08-05 12:39:03 ciphertrust CipherTrust: 2019-08-05 12:39:03 ciphertrust LEEF:2|Thales Group|CipherTrust|Development|Update Syslog Connection|{"name":"Update Syslog Connection","sev":"6","details":"'Update Syslog Connection' succeeded ({"createdAt":"2019-08-12T06:20:06.926665Z","details":{"id":"e847e529-d331-45f9-a494-83ee7ce6ab69"},"message":"Update Syslog Connection","service":"kylo","success":true,"username":"admin","severity":"info","clientIP":"","source":""})
```

The first time stamp is generated and added by syslog and the second time
stamp is the time of the actual audit record.

In a multi-node clustered environment the syslog connections
configuration will be automatically synchronized and each node will be
aware of all syslog servers. The syslog message will be sent from the
currently active node. This means that if an event that results in an
audit record is performed on node 1 the syslog message will originate
from node 1, in a similar manner if an audit event is performed on node 2
the syslog message will in this case originate from node 2.

Please note that it can take up to 5 minutes before the syslog
connections configuration is applied to all nodes in the cluster.

Cluster.description:
A `cluster` is a group of one or more system `nodes` that synchronize their data. A `cluster` is
initially created on a single system, which becomes the first node in the cluster. Additional nodes
can then be added. The full sequence for creating a two node cluster is:

1. POST `/cluster/new` on the initial node.  This creates a one node cluster.
2. POST `/cluster/csr` on the new node to get a CSR.
3. POST `/nodes` with the CSR to the member node to get a cert and chain.
4. POST `/cluster/join` on the new node with the cert and chain to join the node to the cluster.

Additional nodes can be joined in the same way by repeating steps 2,3 and 4. Note that on some calls a hostname is
required. This must be a hostname or IP address that nodes in the cluster can use to contact each other.  

The cluster uses the RAFT consensus algorithm to build consensus among nodes. 
Nodes in cluster use 2380 port for RAFT Consensus communication, firewalls should allow 2380 port within nodes.

Cluster Nodes.description:
The Cluster Nodes API is used for creating new nodes, getting information about existing nodes, and for deleting nodes. When
deleting a node, the DELETE must be send to a node other than the one being deleting.  This will cause replication
to stop to the deleted node, which should be destroyed.

Backups/Backup-Restore.description:
Backups are a snapshot of the data in a system at a point in time. They are created on the system,
and after creation they can be used to restore the system to a previous state, or to transfer data
from one system to another. When a backup is created, it starts an asynchronous backup operation. The status of
a backup can be checked with a GET request. Backups are encrypted with a `backup key`. They can then
be stored externally or transferred to another system. You must transfer the backup key to the target system before
restoring an encrypted backup.

Partial domain backup supports different types of resources to be backed up. Resources supported are "Keys", "cte_policies", "customer_fragments" and "users_groups".

In case of Partial domain backup of keys, it is recommended to always backup all versions of keys.

**WARNING:** Taking backups of selective or only latest version of keys can lead to situation where data encrypted with non-backed up version is not possible to decrypt.
To backup all versions of specific keys, use names. Sample request: `"resourceQuery": {"names" : ["key1", "key2"]}`

Backups/SCP Backup.description:
The APIs in this section are used to copy backup to the external servers using Secure Copy Protocol (SCP)
or Simple File Transfer Protocol (SFTP).

The following operations can be performed:
- Get SCP/SFTP public key
- Copy backup to remote host machine
- Get backup SCP/SFTP status

Supported auth methods for SCP/SFTP connections are key and password.
For the auth method key, the user must download the public key from scp/publickey API and append it to the destination host machine's authorized keys,
And for the auth method password user can provide the destination host machine password.

User also need to provide host public key for verification, which can be located at "/etc/ssh/" at destination host machine.

Backup Keys.description:
A backup key encrypts a backup file. A backup key includes two keys: an AES 256 encryption key and a HMAC SHA-256 signing key.
A default backup key is created for each system, and additional keys can be created as needed. To
restore a backup to a different system, download the backup key used to encrypt the backup,
and then upload the key to the target system. A password is required to protect the backup key when it is downloaded
from the system.

Certificate Authority.description:
A Certificate Authority (CA) issues and installs digital certificates and
certificate signing requests (CSR).

A certificate generally acts as the identity of a server or client and
this API can be used to issue server and client certificates in order to
setup trusted communication channels to the system. A Certificate
Authority acts as the initially trusted shared entity between peers and
can issue signed certificates to make it possible for each party to trust
the other.

The system distinguishes between local CAs and external CAs with the
difference that a local CA can issue signed certificates as the private
signing key is stored inside the system. An external CA does not store
the private key and can instead be used as a trusted entity for various
interfaces and services inside the system when certificates are issued
externally. It is fine to have a mix of both.

During initial bootstrapping of a new server a new local `CipherTrust Manager root
CA` is automatically generated. This CA is later used to issue a server
certificate for the interfaces available in the system. An easy way to
inspect the certificate chain is to view the certificates in your browser
when you connect to the web interface. All interfaces and services will
by default trust this CA which means that a client certificate issued
from this initial `CipherTrust Manager root CA` will automatically be trusted by
the system. If preferred it is possible to create new local CAs and/or
external CAs and instead used them for the internal interfaces and
services.

Creating a local CA is a two step process:
 1. Invoke `Create local CA` which creates a local CA in `pending` state
    and returns a CSR for signing.
 2. A `pending` local CA can then be activated in two ways:
    - Invoke `Self-sign a local CA` to let the CA sign itself. This is
      typically done for Root CAs.
    - Invoke `Install a local CA` which requires a signed certificate
      based on the CSR from the `pending` CA. This certificate can be
      signed by any other entity such as an external CA or even an other
      local CA.

Once a local CA exists a signed certificate can be issued in two steps:
1. Invoke `CSR` to create a CSR and private key. It is also possible to
   create the CSR and the private key using any other software as this API
   is stateless and doesn't store anything in the system.
2. Invoke `Issue certificate` and provide the CSR, the purpose and the
   duration. A new signed certificate will be returned.

CipherTrust Manager allows to revoke and resume certificates signed by local CA.
User can specify a reason to revoke a certificate according to RFC 5280.
Certificates revoked with `certificateHold` reason will only allow resuming.

Creating an external CA is a single step:
1. Invoke `Upload external CA` and provide the signed external CA
   certificate.

Links.description:
Links are a way to associate key objects. This implementation is based on the KMIP standard,
and so there are specific types of Links:

- privateKey
- publicKey
- certificate
- derivationBaseObject
- derivedKey
- replacementObject
- replacedObject
- parent
- child
- previous
- next
- pkcs12Password
- pkcs12Certificate

A link must have a type (one of the above), a source, and a target. For example, if a Link
has a source of key1, a target of key2, and a type of `publicKey`, it means that: key2 is the public
key associated with key1 (which is presumably a private key). Links are uni-directional, so in the previous
example there will be another link of type `privateKey`, with a source of key2, and target of key1.
In KMIP calls, links appear as attributes associated with the source object.

For convenience, links will also appear as a read-only array for objects returned from the Keys API.

NTP Servers.description:
NTP (Network Time Protocol) is used to synchronize time with an external time source.

If at least one NTP server is added CipherTrust Manager will internally start and run the NTP time daemon `ntpd` to set the
system time. It is recommended to configure more than a single NTP server to ensure the time is correct at all
times. Each time an NTP server is added or removed CipherTrust Manager will automatically referesh the internal NTP daemon to
use the new set of NTP servers.

More information about the recommended number of NTP servers can be found on [ntp.org.](http://support.ntp.org/bin/view/Support/SelectingOffsiteNTPServers#Section_5.3.3.)

NTP servers in CipherTrust Manager are uniquely identified by the `host`.

Please note that the NTP server configuration isn't synchronized between servers in a cluster. This means that
any NTP servers must be added to each individual server in the cluster and it also means that it is possible to
have different set of NTP servers in each server.

Network.description:
Tools for testing communications from a CipherTrust Manager system to other
machines via tools that emulate ping, netcat (checkport), traceroute and nslookup.

APIs for managing and retrieving the network interfaces of a CipherTrust Manager
node. An interface supports two families: inet (IPv4) and inet6 (IPv6). A
family may be disabled or configured to use either static values or
dynamic values (e.g. via DHCP).  All addresses returned in a response are
live values even if the network interface is configured dynamically.

Please note there is a risk that modifying a network interface remotely
using this API may make communication with the node impossible without
console access.

MKek.description:
MKek is Master Key Encryption Key. The Key is common across multiple nodes
in a cluster and is used as a master key to protect the secrets in a CipherTrust Manager.
The interface provides APIs to manage MKek. The following operation can be performed on MKek
- List MKek : Lists the mkeks.
- Get MKek : Gets the mkek by ID.
- Rotate MKek : Rotates the default mkek which creates a new mkek across the nodes in a cluster
as well as in a non-cluster node.

HSM Servers.description:
HSM (Hardware Security Module) is a physical device for more secure
management of sensitive data, such as keys, inside CipherTrust Manager. These set
of APIs allows for dynamic configuration of the HSM servers used.

Supported HSM types are `luna`, `lunatct`, `lunapci`, `protectserver`, `aws`, `dpod`, `gcp`, `nshield` and `ibmhpcs`.

Before you can integrate an HSM with CipherTrust Manager, some configuration
is needed on the HSM to allow CipherTrust Manager to connect. The necessary values
are described in the `connInfo` and `initialConfig` schemas. Consult documentation for the particular
HSM product and version for more information on creating the needed passwords, certificates,
and string values.

During initial setup a `reset` operation is required to perform an
initial bootstrap of the CipherTrust Manager using the HSM. This means that all
existing data in the system will be wiped and CipherTrust Manager will be stared
from a clean slate.

After the initial HSM setup it is possible to add further HSMs for
high-availability (HA). Adding further HSMs doesn't require a reset as
data will be synchronized from the other HSMs in the HA group. When the
second HSM is added a HA group will automatically be created and will
require a `restart` operation for all connections to start to use the HA
group.  Without the restart all existing connections will use the
initially configured HSM and the server won't fully utilize the HA
feature.

Please note that these APIs can have a big impact on the availability of
CipherTrust Manager and the data inside it. It should be used with great care and
clear intentions. It is always recommended to take a backup before using
these APIs.

Info.description:
These endpoints allow the user to query for some basic information from
CipherTrust Manager - the name, version and model number, vendor of the platform.

It is also possible to update the platform name to something that is
illustrative to the user.

Disk Encryption.description:
For added security, the disk of the CipherTrust Manager system can be fully encrypted.

Following are APIs for management of the encryption status of hard disks.  It supports
operations to retrieve the status of the disk and to encrypt the disk at next boot.

These APIs are only accessible after first boot; if the user desires to encrypt
the disk before first boot the cloud-init methods must be used.

Migrations.description:
This API can be used for migrating backups taken on 'KeySecure Classic' or 'DSM'  (Data Security Manager) devices onto the newer CipherTrust Manager devices.
The backup file should be uploaded before migration.
The uploaded backup files can be listed and deleted.
The migration is performed asynchronously. The state of the ongoing migration can be monitored.
A 'KeySecure Classic' backup file is protected by a password, and the password is specified when migrating the backup file.
A 'DSM' backup file is protected by a 'Migration Split Key'. The 'Migration Split Keys' API should be used
for uploading these keys. These keys must be uploaded before the backup is migrated.

Alarms.description:
The alarms API displays the state of CipherTrust Manager alarms. Each alarm has a unique name. Examples of alarm state
are on, off, unknown, etc. Each alarm has a severity, which are listed below.

CDP.description: The CDP APIs can be used for adding and updating database migration information for CipherTrust Database Protection(CDP) clients.

SNMP.description:
This API can be used for configuring SNMP management stations (notification receivers), Community names and
SNMPv3 USM users for managing and monitoring the CipherTrust Manager using SNMP protocol.
SNMP versions v1, v2c and v3 are supported.

SNMP interface is not started by default. It can be started from 'Settings | Interfaces' GUI, API or CLI.
It must be started before using this API.

CTE.description:
CipherTrust Transparent Encryption (CTE) delivers data-at-rest encryption with centralized key management, privileged user access control, and detailed data access audit logging. This protects data wherever it resides—on-premises, across multiple clouds, and within big data.

CTE:
  - Encrypts files and raw data
  - Controls which users can decrypt and access that data
  - Controls which processes and executables can decrypt and encrypt that data
  - Generates fine-grained audit trails on those processes, executables, and users

CTE/Clients.description:
A client is a computer system where the data needs to be protected. A compatible CTE Agent software is installed on the client. The CTE Agent can protect data on the client or devices connected to it. A client can be associated with multiple GuardPoints for encryption of various paths.

*OPERATIONS* *On* *Client*:

        UnEnroll:

              - A CTE client with Active LDT GuardPoints cannot be unenrolled (unregistered).

              - After unenrolling, the client's GuardPoints will still be displayed on the CipherTrust Manager. However, their status will be displayed as Unknown.

              - The status of the client capabilities, for example, LDT will not change on the CipherTrust Manager. They will be displayed the same as they were before unenrolling the client.

              - The associated client under the Client-Management section is deleted after unenrolling. If the client is not deleted automatically, you can delete it manually.

              - The status of the unenrolled client will be displayed as Unregistered on the CipherTrust Manager.

        Delete:

              - Waits for the confirmation from the Agent before deleting anything on the CTE client.

              - Deletes all entries, capabilities, and GuardPoints associated with the client.

              - Deletes the associated client from the Client-Management section of the API playground.

*STATES* *Of* *Client*:

      1. Healthy: Client is registered with the CipherTrust Manager without any errors, that is, `init` is received from Agent without any issues. The client's status on the CipherTrust Manager is displayed as HEALTHY.

      2. Warning: Client's communication is broken with the CipherTrust Manager or a GuardPoint is inactive due to any reasons. The client's status on the CipherTrust Manager is displayed as WARNING.

      3. Error: Client's communication is broken with the CipherTrust Manager for more than five minutes. The client's status on the CipherTrust Manager is displayed as ERROR.

      4. Unregistered: Client is unenrolled from the CipherTrust Manager. The client's status on the CipherTrust Manager is displayed as UNREGISTERED.

      5. Expunged: Client's delete operation is triggered, but its confirmation is not yet received from the Agent. The client's status on the CipherTrust Manager is displayed as EXPUNGED.

CTE/ClientGroups.description:
A client group is used to group one or more clients to simplify configuration and administration. GuardPoints created on a client group are applied to all members of the group. Additionally, you can apply client group configuration settings (except the password, Agent Lock, System Lock, and Communication Enabled settings) to all clients in a client group.
CTE supports non-clustered client groups. A non-clustered client group contains members that are not members of a cluster. A client can be a member of multiple client groups.

CTE/ClientGroups-GuardPoints.description: A GuardPoint specifies the list of folders that contains paths to be protected. Access to files and encryption of files under the GuardPoint is controlled by security policies. GuardPoints created on a client group are applied to all members of the group.

CTE/CloudObjectStorage.description: CTE can encrypt data and apply access rules on the GuardPoints in the cloud. CTE supports Amazon S3 buckets.

CTE/Policies.description:
A policy is a collection of rules that govern data access and encryption. Think of a policy as an if-then statement. Policy rules are processed sequentially. If the criteria of rule one are not met, the policy enforcement engine moves on to the second rule and so on.

Policies specify:
- Actors: Users, groups, and processes that are permitted/denied access to protected data.
- Actions: What actions authorized actors are allowed to perform. For example create/delete, read/write, decrypt, modify permissions, and so on.
- Files acted upon: Policy rules may apply to entire directories and mount points, or only to files named in a specific way (for example,.docx files may be encrypted and restricted to read‐only access by designated users, while other files may be stored clear and read and written by anyone).

**Note:** All keys which are applicable to be used in CTE policies need to have certain CTE specific parameters under the Key meta section. Refer **Keys** section for complete details

**Types** **of** **Policies**:

        STANDARD POLICY:
        A STANDARD policy should contain security rules and/or key rules. At least one of these rules must be added to the standard policy.The security rules define the access permissions based on the policy elements (user sets, resource set, and process sets). The key rules define what key is used for encryption and decryption of data.

        LIVE DATA TRANSFORMATION(LDT) POLICY:
        An LDT policy should contain at least one non-exclusion key rule. The security rules define the access permissions based on the policy elements (user sets, resource set, and process sets).An LDT policy has two sets of keys, one is the current key and the other is transformation key.

           - Current key: The key with which the data is encrypted before any transformation. If the data is in plaintext, then the current key should be set as "clear_key".

           - Transformation key: The key with which the data is to be encrypted. This key must be VERSIONED so that multiple key versions can be created as and when required.

        CLOUD OBJECT STORAGE(COS) POLICY:
        A COS policy should contain security rules and/or key rules. At least one of these rules must be added to the COS policy.The security rules define the access permissions based on the policy elements (user sets, resource set, and process sets). The key rules define what key is used for encryption and decryption of data.

            *NOTE*: COS policies support the "CBC_CS1" keys only.

        In-PLACE DATA TRANSFORMATION(IDT) POLICY:
        An IDT policy should contain security rules and/or key rules. At least one of these rules must be added to the standard policy.The security rules define the access permissions based on the policy elements (user sets, resource set, and process sets). The key rules define what key is used for encryption and decryption of data.

            *NOTE*: IDT policies support the "XTS" keys only.

        CONTAINER STORAGE INTERFACE(CSI) POLICY:
        A CSI policy applicable to GuardPolicies for CTE Kubernetes (K8s) clients. Access to data is blocked during initial encryption or rekeying of data. This policy is similar to the Standard policy with the following limitations:
        * Signature sets are not supported.

            *NOTE*: For Container Storage Interface (CSI) policies, select a CBC-CS1 key. CSI policies do not support XTS and CBC keys.

CTE/Policies-DataTxRules.description:
Data transformation (dataxform) rules define:
- Resources to be protected
- Symmetric encryption key to use for
  - Rekeying the specified resources from one encryption key to a different key or
  - Rekeying resources into a plaintext format (also referred to as clear, unencrypted, or decrypted)

CTE/Policies-KeyRules.description:
A key rule defines the encryption key to apply to a specific resource set or the encryption key to use as the
default key, if no other key rule matches. The key rule defines the sequence in which the key rules are to be
executed (Order), the location of the data to be encrypted (Resource), and the encryption key to be applied to
the resource set (Key).

When defining a key rule for an LDT policy, you can select a key that is applied to the resource set (Current Key
Name) and the key to use to rekey that resource set (Transformation Key Name).

CTE/Policies-LDTRules.description:
Live data transformation rules define:
Resources to be protected.

Symmetric encryption key to use for:
  - Rekeying the specified resources from one encryption key to a different key.
  - Rekeying resources into a plaintext format (also referred to as clear, unencrypted, or decrypted).

CTE/Policies-IDTRules.description:
In-Place data transformation rules define:

Symmetric encryption key to use for:
  - Rekeying the specified resources on a raw device from one encryption key to a different key.

CTE/Policies-SecurityRules.description:
A security rule defines who can access the data (User or Group), what they can do with the data (Action), which
applications or executables have access to the data (Process), where the data is located (Resource), how the
data can be accessed (Effect), and whether it can be viewed from the CipherTrust Manager (Browsing).

CTE/Profiles.description:
A profile contains the CipherTrust Manager logging criteria for CTE clients, Syslog server configuration, default logging level, LDT Quality of Service (QoS) settings, and other settings that can be used for several CTE clients. A default profile, DefaultClientProfile, is created automatically when either of the following happens:

- On successful registration of the first client if no profile is specified during registration.
- On creation of the first client group. A new client group is automatically linked to DefaultClientProfile.

When registering a CTE client, the installer prompts to specify a profile for the client. If not specified, DefaultClientProfile is automatically linked to the client on successful registration. The linked profile can be modified later. It is recommended to not delete or modify DefaultClientProfile.

CTE/ProcessSets.description:
A process set is a collection of processes (executables) that you want to grant or deny access to GuardPoints. This provides a way to manage processes independent of the policy. Policies can be applied to process sets, not to individual processes.
Optionally, file signing can be configured to check the authenticity and integrity of executables and applications before they are allowed to access GuardPoint data. A signature set must already exist before you can configure file signing in a policy for a process set.

CTE/ResourceSets.description:
A resource is a combination of a directory, a file, and patterns or special variables. A resource set is a named
collection of directories, files, or both, that a user or process will be permitted or denied access to.

CTE/SignatureSets.description:
A signature set is a collection of hashes of processes and executables that you want to grant or deny access to GuardPoints. A signature set can be configured in a policy as part of a process set to verify the integrity of a process before it is allowed access to guarded data. Policies are applied to signature sets, not to individual signatures.

**Note:**
- K8 resources supported are: Pods, Deployment, ReplicaSet, StatefulSets, DaemonSet
- Following is the sample YAML file for testing /v1/transparent-encryption/signaturesets/{signatureSetId}/upload-yaml API:
```
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: ReplicaSet
metadata:
  name: frontend
  labels:
    app: guestbook
    tier: frontend
spec:
  replicas: 3
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      tier: frontend
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        tier: frontend
    spec:
      containers:
        - name: php-redis
          image: gcr.io/google_samples/gb-frontend:v3
```

CTE/UserSets.description: A user set is a collection of users and user groups that you want to grant or deny access to GuardPoints. User sets are configured in policies. Policies can be applied to user sets, not to individual users.

CTE/LDTGroupCommServices.description:
An LDT group communication service contains a group of LDT-enabled CTE clients that can communicate with each other. An LDT group communication service is mandatory when using a multi-node solution for LDT over NFS/CIFS. The CipherTrust Manager pushes the LDT group details to all clients in the group.

**Note:**

- The LDT group communication services are applicable to the LDT-enabled CTE clients.
- A client can be added to only one LDT group communication service at a time.
- For successful communication among clients in an LDT group communication service, make sure that clients are registered with the CipherTrust Manager using their hostnames or IP addresses.

**WARNING:** All the clients guarding a common share must be part of the same LDT group communication service, otherwise, data may be corrupted. If you need to change the LDT group of a client, ensure that the client no longer guards the common share.

For example, if 10 clients will be guarding a common share, add all of them to the same LDT group communication service only. To change the LDT group communication service of one of these clients, ensure that the client no longer guards the share. However, to change the LDT group of all 10 clients, it is recommended to take the GuardPoint offline, change the LDT group, and reapply the GuardPoint.

CTE/CSIStorageGroups.description: This section contains APIs for managing Storage Group resources related to Kubernetes Container Storage Interface (CSI).

CTE/K8sRegistrationGroups.description: This section contains APIs for managing Registration Group resources related to K8s Cloud Object Storage (COS).

CTE/Permissions.description:
This API is used to display the list of permissions for all the CTE resources, for example, Clients, Policies, Signatures and GuardPoints etc. Most of the resources require read, update, and delete permissions. Example of the permissions required by clients and policies resources are given below:

Resource Type    |    Actions           |    Description
---------------- |    ------------------|    -----------
clients          |    ReadClientCTE     |    Permission to read the CTE clients.
clients          |    UpdateClientCTE   |    Permission to update the CTE clients.
clients          |    DeleteClientCTE   |    Permission to delete the CTE clients.
policies         |    ReadPolicyCTE     |    Permission to read the CTE policies.
policies         |    UpdatePolicyCTE   |    Permission to update the CTE policies.
policies         |    DeletePolicyCTE   |    Permission to delete the CTE policies.

CTE/Reports.description:
This section contains APIs for fetching CTE reports. A report contains informaton related to association of CTE clients, policies, keys, guardpoints and profiles.
Reports can be fetched system wide or domain specific.

For fetching system wide reports user must be member of either `admin` or `CTE Admins` group and for domain specific report `domain_name` filter param is required.

For example assuming below as CipherTrust Manager domain hierarchy, fetching system wide report will return reports from `root, domain1 and domain1_child` domains.

Sample output of client health system wide report:
